# Editorial overview

## Read before code: problem dossiers

**A. Scoreboard Rank.** Reduce each row to `(-solved, penalty, name)` and sort.
That tuple is the stated tie rule; test exact ties and lexicographic names.
Complexity `O(n log n)`.

**B. Split Workload.** Every subset is one teammate's task set and its complement
is the other's. Enumerating all masks covers every split; minimize the larger
sum. Test one task and an exactly balanced split. Complexity `O(n2^n)` locally.

**C. Quick MST Decision.** Kruskal's accepted edges cross DSU components, so
the cut property yields a minimum spanning tree. Test disconnected inputs and
equal weights before interpreting savings.

## Problem-specific proof map

**A. Scoreboard Rank.** The stored tuple `(-solved, penalty, name)` is exactly
the lexicographic contest ranking rule, so sorting those tuples gives the
required order in `O(n log n)`.

**B. Split Workload.** Every assignment of tasks to one teammate is one subset;
enumerating all subsets therefore examines every two-way split and minimizes
the larger load exactly.

**C. Quick MST Decision.** Kruskal's DSU rejects cycle edges and accepts only
component-merging edges. Its cut-property proof gives the minimum network and
therefore the requested savings decision.

**D. Circular Contest Run.** Duplicate the circular order conceptually and
maintain the longest affordable window, never allowing more than `n` items.
Positive times make the two-pointer left boundary monotone.

## Detailed solution guide

**A. Scoreboard Sorting.** Store each team by solved count, penalty, and name.
The comparator sorts by more solved problems first, lower penalty second, and
lexicographic name last. This mirrors the statement exactly, so once every team
record is computed, sorting produces the required ranking.

**B. Subset Partition Drill.** The problem is a small knapsack/subset-sum
decision. Maintain reachable sums after processing each item. Initially only
sum `0` is reachable. For each value, update sums in descending order so the
value is used at most once. The best partition is the reachable sum closest to
half the total.

**C. MST Decision Drill.** Build the minimum spanning tree with Kruskal. If the
MST weight is at most the budget, print feasible; otherwise not. The cut
property ensures Kruskal gives the cheapest connected network, so no other
spanning tree can fit the budget when the MST does not.

**Common pitfalls.** In contest workflow problems, the algorithms are often
standard; the challenge is reading carefully, choosing the right template, and
testing boundary cases before moving on.

These exercises are small contest-operation drills.

- A implements scoreboard ordering exactly: more solved first, lower penalty
  second, name as deterministic tiebreak.
- B is subset/partition search for balancing workload between two solvers.
- C recognizes MST savings quickly: total edge weight minus MST weight if the
  graph is connected.

The editorial emphasis is precision under time pressure: model the rule, test
corner cases, then code the smallest reliable version.

# A. Scoreboard Rank

## Restatement

Sort teams by more solved, then lower penalty, then name.

## Observations and algorithm

Store each team as `(-solved, penalty, name)` and sort tuples. This encodes the
ranking rule directly; trace two teams tied on solves but not penalty, then a
complete tie resolved by name.

## Correctness proof

Tuple lexicographic order compares exactly the stated tie-break fields in their
required priority, so sorted output is the requested scoreboard. $\square$

## Complexity

Sorting is `O(n log n)` time and `O(n)` memory. Avoid sorting names before
negating solved count.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n;if(!(cin>>n))return 0;vector<tuple<int,int,string>>v;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){string s;int a,b;cin>>s>>a>>b;v.push_back({-a,b,s});}sort(v.begin(),v.end());for(auto [a,b,s]:v)cout<<s<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def main():
    lines=sys.stdin.read().splitlines()
    if not lines: return
    rows=[]
    for line in lines[1:]:
        name,sol,pen=line.split(); rows.append((-int(sol),int(pen),name))
    rows.sort(); print("\n".join(name for _,_,name in rows))
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

# B. Split Workload

## Restatement

Split problem times between two solvers minimizing the maximum load.

## Observations and algorithm

For each mask, one solver receives selected tasks and the other receives its
complement. Enumerating every mask covers every split; update the answer with
the smaller maximum load. Test one task and an exactly balanced subset.

## Correctness proof

Every legal two-person allocation determines exactly one subset, and every mask
determines one allocation, so taking the minimum examines the optimum. $\square$

## Complexity

The local brute force is `O(n2^n)` time; it is intentionally limited to small
n. Use a running subset sum rather than recomputing it in harder variants.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n;if(!(cin>>n))return 0;vector<int>a(n);int tot=0;for(int&x:a){cin>>x;tot+=x;}int best=1e9;for(int m=0;m<(1<<n);m++){int s=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if(m>>i&1)s+=a[i];best=min(best,max(s,tot-s));}cout<<best<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def main():
    data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data: return
    n=data[0]; a=data[1:]; best=10**9
    for mask in range(1<<n):
        s=sum(a[i] for i in range(n) if mask>>i&1); best=min(best,max(s,sum(a)-s))
    print(best)
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

# C. Quick MST Decision

## Restatement

Use MST savings as a contest modeling drill.

## Observations and algorithm

Sort edges and use DSU exactly as Kruskal: accepted edges merge components,
rejected edges close cycles. Compare the resulting MST cost with the requested
decision/budget only after checking connectivity.

## Correctness proof

The cut property makes each component-merging minimum edge safe; therefore no
connected subgraph can cost less than the constructed tree. $\square$

## Complexity

Time `O(m log m)`, memory `O(n)`. Test a disconnected graph and equal-weight
edges; do not interpret a forest as a feasible network.

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std; int main(){ios::sync_with_stdio(false);cin.tie(nullptr);int n,m;if(!(cin>>n>>m))return 0;vector<array<int,3>>e;long long total=0;for(int i=0,a,b,w;i<m;i++){cin>>a>>b>>w;e.push_back({w,a-1,b-1});total+=w;}vector<int>p(n);iota(p.begin(),p.end(),0);function<int(int)>f=[&](int x){return p[x]==x?x:p[x]=f(p[x]);};sort(e.begin(),e.end());long long keep=0;int cnt=0;for(auto [w,a,b]:e){a=f(a);b=f(b);if(a!=b){p[a]=b;keep+=w;cnt++;}}cout<<(cnt==n-1?total-keep:-1)<<'\n';}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys
def main():
    data=list(map(int,sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data: return
    n,m=data[0],data[1]; edges=[]; total=0; idx=2
    for _ in range(m):
        a,b,w=data[idx],data[idx+1],data[idx+2]; idx+=3; edges.append((w,a-1,b-1)); total+=w
    p=list(range(n))
    def f(x):
        while p[x]!=x: p[x]=p[p[x]]; x=p[x]
        return x
    keep=0; cnt=0
    for w,a,b in sorted(edges):
        ra,rb=f(a),f(b)
        if ra!=rb: p[ra]=rb; keep+=w; cnt+=1
    print(total-keep if cnt==n-1 else -1)
if __name__=="__main__": main()
```

# D. Circular Contest Run

## Restatement and modeling

Choose a start in a circular list and take a consecutive clockwise block whose
total time fits the budget. No problem may be taken twice. Trying every start
and extending separately is quadratic.

Conceptually concatenate the list with itself. Every circular block of at most
`n` problems is now an ordinary interval in that doubled sequence. Because all
times are positive, removing items from the left can only decrease its sum.

## Sliding-window algorithm

Maintain an inclusive window `[left,right]` and its total time while `right`
moves through `0..2n-1`:

```text
add time[right mod n]
while total > budget or window length > n:
    remove time[left mod n]
    left += 1
answer = max(answer, window length)
```

The length condition prevents walking around the circle more than once. For
`[4,2,1,5,2]` with budget 8, windows of length three include `[4,2,1]` and the
wrap-free `[1,5,2]`; no length-four window fits.

## Correctness proof

For each fixed right endpoint, after the while-loop the window is affordable,
has length at most `n`, and has the smallest possible left endpoint with those
properties. Any earlier left endpoint violates the sum or length constraint.
Therefore this is the longest valid interval ending at `right`.

Every legal circular block appears as an interval of length at most `n` in the
doubled sequence, with an endpoint before `2n`. When that endpoint is
processed, the maintained window is at least as long as the block ending
there. Taking the maximum thus finds an optimum, and every considered window
maps back to a legal circular block. $\square$

## Complexity and tests

Each doubled position enters once and leaves at most once, so time is `O(n)`
and memory is `O(n)` for the input. Use 64-bit sums. Test budget zero, one item,
an answer wrapping across the last/first boundary, budget covering all items,
and the `n`-item length cap.
